newsitem.title: INDIA: Troubled Kashmir prepares to go to polls.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Kashmir prepares to go to polls.

text.p: Kashmir this weekend launches the first phase of local assembly polls which India hopes will foreshadow an end to a violent six-year-old separatist revolt that has fanned regional tensions.

Authorities said 200,000 soldiers, paramilitary troops and police would be deployed in Jammu and Kashmir state for the first local polls since the start of the insurgency, in which some 20,000 people have been killed.
The elections to the Himalayan state's 87-seat assembly begin on Saturday and will be held in stages over four days, ending on September 30.
Militants have threatened violence.
The polls are being held four months after Indian parliamentary elections in the state were marred by allegations that security forces coerced some voters into casting ballots.
Authorities denied the claims.

The general elections thrust a new government into power in New Delhi. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition quickly seized the chance to hold the first local polls in Jammu and Kashmir since 1987.
Last year, Deve Gowda's predecessor, P.V. Narasimha Rao at the head of the Congress party, made two aborted attempts to hold local polls in the state.
The first collapsed in mid-1995 when the mostly Moslem region's holiest shrine in Charar-e-Sharief went up in flames following a clash between security forces and militants.
The second attempt ran into opposition from the federal Election Commission, which ruled late last year that the threat of violence by militants prevented free and fair polls.
Authorities say militancy in mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state has abated since then and Kashmiris are tired of a rebellion that has strangled the local economy, especially tourism.
"We have crushed the militancy and created conditions favourable for the holding of elections," state Governor K.V. Krishna Rao told Reuters Television in an interview this week.
"People are fed up. Now they see light at the end of the tunnel," he said.
Krishna Rao said 40,000 to 50,000 security reinforcements had been sent to the state, raising the number of forces engaged in anti-militancy operations and poll protection duties to about 200,000.
Separatists say the forces have mounted a crackdown.
Deve Gowda's bid to restore normalcy to the state was boosted when the leading pro-India party, the National Conference, decided to participate in this month's polls.

Its leader, Farooq Abdullah, had refused to take part in the parliamentary elections in May but was enticed into the fray this time by a government promise to offer the state "maximum autonomy" after the polls.
Krishna Rao predicted the turnout could range between 50 and 60 percent, up from some 45 percent in the parliamentary polls.
The All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which includes some 30 leading separatist groups, has called on voters to boycott the elections.
But the Hurriyat, whose members favour independence or merger with neighbouring Pakistan, is hobbled by internal splits and mounting frustration with militancy, diplomats say.
"We think the Kashmiris are sick of it and want life to get back to normal," one foreign diplomat said.

A senior British official travelling with Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind to India said last week there were hopes that India and arch-foe Pakistan could resume high-level bilateral talks, suspended in early 1994, following the polls.
Two of the three wars fought by India and Pakistan since independence in 1947 have been over Kashmir. Pakistan has denied India's accusations that it arms and trains militants.
"There is some scope for limited expansion of contact between Pakistan and India once the elections are over. Whether there will be real dialogue, we have to be cautious," the British official said.
